headline: Museum fossil reveals prehistoric predator after 75 years of silence
meta_description: A forgotten fossil from Ghost Ranch in New Mexico reveals a new Triassic predator species that lived 210 million years ago alongside early crocodile relatives.
summary_short: Yale paleontologists identified a new species from a fossil overlooked for 75 years, showing how early crocodile relatives hunted in different ways.
body:
A fossil that sat unstudied in a Yale museum for nearly 80 years has finally revealed its secrets: a jackal-sized predator that walked the riverbanks of northern New Mexico 210 million years ago. Named Eosphorosuchus lacrimosa, the animal had a short, heavily reinforced skull and powerful jaw muscles built for tackling larger prey—a striking contrast to its neighbor, Hesperosuchus agilis, which had a longer snout and was built for speed. Both creatures died together, possibly in a flash flood, and their remains were preserved side by side in rock at the Peabody Museum of Natural History at Yale. The discovery matters because it shows that even closely related predators were already dividing up food resources by developing different hunting strategies during the late Triassic period.

Yale paleontologist Bhart-Anjan Bhullar noticed the difference in the animal's facial structure while examining it, prompting a closer investigation. Miranda Margulis-Ohnuma, a Ph.D. student, used CT scans to examine bones still embedded in rock, digitally reconstructing the fossil one bone at a time. Those scans revealed anatomical features distinct enough to classify the animal as a separate species entirely—one that had somehow escaped formal identification for decades despite being housed in one of the world's leading museums.

The find underscores something both humbling and hopeful: existing museum collections continue to yield discoveries without requiring new excavations. Ghost Ranch's exceptionally preserved fossils have attracted scientists for a century, yet they still hold secrets. Eosphorosuchus stands as one of only a handful of well-preserved early crocodile relatives, offering a rare window into a moment when the ancestors of today's crocodiles were becoming more diverse, more specialized, and more successful—long before dinosaurs would dominate the world.
quick_facts: Fossil overlooked for nearly 80 years in Yale museum
Named Eosphorosuchus lacrimosa; lived 210 million years ago
Found at Ghost Ranch in northern New Mexico
CT scans revealed anatomy hidden in rock
Two predator species coexisted, hunted differently
